Square Breathing (Box Breathing): A Simple Technique for Panic Attacks

When anxiety or panic starts to rise, square breathing can help slow your breathing and calm your body’s stress response.

⬜ Step 1: Breathe in through your nose for 4 seconds
⬜ Step 2: Hold your breath for 4 seconds
⬜ Step 3: Breathe out slowly through your mouth for 4 seconds
⬜ Step 4: Hold your breath again for 4 seconds

Repeat this cycle for 1–3 minutes or until you feel calmer.

Why it helps:
During a panic attack, breathing often becomes rapid and shallow. Square breathing encourages slow, controlled breaths, which can reduce physical symptoms such as a racing heart, dizziness, and feelings of panic.

Remember: Panic attacks are uncomfortable but not dangerous. Controlled breathing can help your body regain a sense of balance and control.

🧠 PTSD: Trauma Doesn’t Have to Define Your Future

A frightening accident, physical assault, abuse, war, natural disaster, or the sudden loss of a loved one can leave emotional scars that continue long after the event is over.

Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD) is a genuine medical condition—not a sign of weakness. It affects how the brain processes fear, memory, and emotions, and it can interfere with work, relationships, sleep, and daily life.

⚠️ Common Symptoms
• Recurrent flashbacks or nightmares
• Avoiding reminders of the trauma
• Feeling emotionally numb or detached
• Irritability or anger outbursts
• Hypervigilance (always “on guard”)
• Poor sleep and concentration
• Feelings of guilt, shame, or hopelessness

💚 The Good News? PTSD is Treatable.

Evidence-based treatments such as:
✅ Trauma-focused Cognitive Behaviour Therapy (CBT)
✅ EMDR (Eye Movement Desensitization & Reprocessing)
✅ Appropriate medications (when needed)
✅ Stress management and lifestyle changes
can significantly improve recovery and quality of life.

🧠 Do You Find Yourself Repeatedly Pulling Your Hair? It Could Be Trichotillomania.

Hair pulling is not simply a "bad habit." For many people, it is a treatable mental health condition called Trichotillomania (Hair Pulling Disorder).

People with trichotillomania often experience:
✔ Repeated pulling of scalp hair, eyebrows, eyelashes, or beard hair
✔ Difficulty controlling the urge despite wanting to stop
✔ Temporary relief after pulling
✔ Visible hair thinning or bald patches
✔ Feelings of embarrassment, guilt, or low confidence

This condition can affect children, teenagers, and adults. Stress, anxiety, boredom, perfectionism, or emotional distress may worsen symptoms.

The good news is that effective treatments are available. Evidence-based approaches such as Habit Reversal Training (HRT), Cognitive Behaviour Therapy (CBT), and appropriate medications when needed can significantly reduce hair-pulling urges and improve quality of life.

Early treatment can prevent progression and help restore confidence.
